question.prompt: A square with an integer side length is cut into \(10\) squares, all of which have integer side length and at least \(8\) of which have area \(1.\) What is the smallest possible value of the length of the side of the original square?

solutions.explanation:
Every small square has a positive integer side length, so each has area at least \(1\). The original square must therefore have area at least \(10\). A square with integer side length at most \(3\) has area at most \(3^2=9\), so the original side length must be at least \(4\).

To show that \(4\) is possible, divide a \(4\)-by-\(4\) square into four \(2\)-by-\(2\) squares. Subdivide two of those squares into four unit squares each, and leave the other two intact.

This gives exactly \(8+2=10\) squares, including eight of area \(1\), and all side lengths are integers. Thus the smallest possible original side length is \(4\), choice \(\text{B}\).
solutions.title: Find a lower bound and attain it
